title: Dispersals and genetic adaptation of Bantu-speaking populations in Africa and North America
authors: Patin E., Lopez M., Grollemund R., Verdu P., Harmant C., et al., Quintana-Murci L.
venue: Science 356: 543-546 (author copy, University of Porto repository)
ask_addressed: Africa: what do linguistics, ancient DNA and archaeology show about the Bantu expansion (dates, routes, Lipson et al. 2020, Patin et al. 2017, Bostoen's work) and what is disputed?
quote: indicate that BSPs first moved southward through the rainforest before migrating toward eastern and southern Africa
summary: Genotyping of 1318 individuals from 35 populations in western central Africa, with present-day data, favours the 'late-split' model: early Bantu speakers moved south through the equatorial rainforest before spreading east and south, admixing with local groups.
limits: Inference from present-day genomes and admixture dating, not ancient DNA. The paper itself frames the expansion as c. 4000-5000 years ago and tests early-split vs late-split; it does not settle the route against the linguistic alternatives. Two-column PDF: quote confirmed on the extracted text.

strand.to: western central, eastern and southern Africa
strand.what: Bantu-speaking populations and their genes, with local admixture

title: Bantu expansion shows that habitat alters the route and pace of human dispersals
authors: Grollemund R., Branford S., Bostoen K., Meade A., Venditti C., Pagel M.
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 112
ask_addressed: Africa: what do linguistics, ancient DNA and archaeology show about the Bantu expansion (dates, routes, Lipson et al. 2020, Patin et al. 2017, Bostoen's work) and what is disputed?
quote: followed emerging savannah corridors, with rainforest habitats repeatedly imposing temporal barriers to movement
summary: A dated phylogeny of about 400 Bantu languages is used to argue that the expansion out of West Central Africa, beginning about 5,000 years ago, followed savannah corridors and that entering rainforest delayed occupation by about 300 years.
limits: Language phylogeny, not DNA or digs; the route depends on the tree topology, which Koile et al. 2022 contest. Co-author Bostoen is also a source in this brief.

title: Phylogeographic analysis of the Bantu language expansion supports a rainforest route
authors: Koile E., Greenhill S.J., Blasi D.E., Bouckaert R., Gray R.D.
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
ask_addressed: Africa: what do linguistics, ancient DNA and archaeology show about the Bantu expansion (dates, routes, Lipson et al. 2020, Patin et al. 2017, Bostoen's work) and what is disputed?
quote: supports the hypothesis of an expansion through Central African tropical forests at 4,420 BP (4,040 to 5,000 95% highest posterior density interval)
summary: A phylogeographic analysis of the Bantu languages compares four hypotheses and favours an early passage through the rainforest, well before the Sangha River Interval savanna corridor opened (c. 2,500 BP), against the corridor model.
limits: Computational reconstruction on a language tree and a chosen set of hypotheses; it is a rival to the savannah-corridor reading, not a settled correction. 'Contradicts' applies to the corridor-led route (Grollemund 2015 in the savannah reading), not to the expansion itself.

strand.from: Bantu homeland north of the rainforest
strand.what: Bantu language family, route and timing

title: Introduction to a New Archaeology of the Bantu Expansion
venue: Chapter 1 in An Archaeology of the Bantu Expansion (Routledge; CC-BY-NC-ND open chapter, Ghent University repository)
ask_addressed: Africa: what do linguistics, ancient DNA and archaeology show about the Bantu expansion (dates, routes, Lipson et al. 2020, Patin et al. 2017, Bostoen's work) and what is disputed?
quote: much uncertainty persists on the chronology and geography of the Bantu Expansion
summary: A specialist overview says Central African archaeology does not contradict linguistics and genetics on a Bantu migration across the Congo rainforest, with sites suggesting roughly the first millennium BCE, but gaps remain. It lists open questions: farming in the rainforest, deforestation versus climate, and whether an Early/Late Iron Age hiatus marks population collapse.
limits: Year not printed on the page I read (the chapter cites 2024 works, so 2024-25). Written by an author whose own project (BantuFirst) is discussed; it surveys rather than tests.

title: Population collapse in Congo rainforest from 400 CE urges reassessment of the Bantu Expansion
authors: Seidensticker D., Hubau W., Verschuren D., Fortes-Lima C., de Maret P., Schlebusch C.M., Bostoen K.
ask_addressed: Africa: what do linguistics, ancient DNA and archaeology show about the Bantu expansion (dates, routes, Lipson et al. 2020, Patin et al. 2017, Bostoen's work) and what is disputed?
quote: separated by a widespread population collapse between 400 and 600 CE followed by major resettlement centuries later
summary: 1149 radiocarbon dates tied to 115 pottery styles from 726 sites show two Iron Age phases split by a population collapse, and the authors conclude with genetic and linguistic evidence that the Bantu dispersal was 'spread-over-spread', not one continuous wave.
limits: Disputed: Bostoen & Coutros (above) cite Clist and others who read the 14C hiatus as a research gap. The proposed epidemic cause is described as 'possible'.

strand.to: Late Iron Age resettlers of the same region

title: Linguistic Evidence for the Introduction of Ironworking into Bantu-Speaking Africa
ask_addressed: Iron working in West Africa (Nok) and its independence or diffusion?
quote: cannot be dated more closely than between 840 and 420 BCE
summary: Vansina says the independent-invention question is 'unresolved and hotly disputed' because the earliest West and West-Central African smelting sites (Taruga and others) cannot be dated more closely than 840-420 BCE on the flat radiocarbon curve; dates before 800 BCE would favour invention, later ones borrowing. He then argues from Bantu vocabulary that ironworking diffused from the north-west.
limits: Published 2006, before the later Nok and Central African dating; the linguistic argument is his own. It does not decide independence versus diffusion.

strand.from: northern West and West-Central Africa (near the Nok area)

title: The Nok of Nigeria
venue: Archaeology (Archaeological Institute of America), vol. 64 no. 4
ask_addressed: Iron working in West Africa (Nok) and its independence or diffusion?
quote: Iron technology was probably brought across the Sahara by travelers from North Africa, says Rod McIntosh
summary: A magazine feature reports a Nok furnace charcoal date of 519-410 BCE at Intini (Breunig) and sets Yale's McIntosh, who favours transmission across the Sahara, against those who suspect autonomous West African invention, possibly starting with the Nok.
limits: Popular outlet: context only, not support for a dating. It reports others' views; the figures come from interviews, not from the excavation reports.

title: Iron metallurgy in Africa
ask_addressed: Iron working in West Africa (Nok) and its independence or diffusion?
quote: Opinion among African archaeologists is sharply divided.
summary: The article summarises the diffusion (Carthage, Meroe) versus independent invention debate, the early Central African Oboui dates (c. 2000 BCE) that Clist calls disturbed while Holl, Craddock and Eggert defend them, and Eggert's 2014 view that independent invention is likely though inconclusive.
limits: Community-edited tertiary summary, read only to map who disputes what; its cited authors (Clist 2012, Eggert 2014, Holl 2020) were not opened. Not support for any date.

strand.from: Mediterranean or Nile Valley (diffusionist view) or none (independent invention)

title: Negus Ezana: Revisiting the Christianisation of Aksum (quoting Ezana's Greek inscription)
ask_addressed: Aksum's adoption of Christianity (Ezana inscriptions; Rufinus)
quote: In the faith of God and the Power of the Father, and the Holy Ghost who have saved my kingdom.
summary: Quotes the Christian Greek inscription of Ezana (after Anfray, Caquot and Nautin 1970) as the clearest evidence of his Christianity, with a pseudo-Sabaean and a Ge'ez version. The author dates the pagan phase to c. 325-333 CE (Munro-Hay) and 333 as a terminus post quem for Christian titulature (Petrides).
limits: An English rendering quoted by a secondary article; I did not read the Greek or the stone. The Ge'ez version is called vague or 'pagan-neutral', and Rukuni argues for a Judaic reading of 'Lord of Heaven'. Verifier: second-hand quotation (Anfray, Caquot & Nautin 1970, quoted through Rukuni), so stance lowered from supports to context and directness from documented to debated; the 333-360 span reports Petrides/Phillipson/Munro-Hay as cited by Rukuni and is itself disputed.
